desc:
Encoding. A singly linked list is passed to your function as an array holding the node values from head to tail; an empty array is an empty list. You may build real nodes from it first, or work on the array directly. Lists you return are given as arrays of values from head to tail.

The list starts and ends with a node of value 0, and no two zeros are adjacent. Between every two consecutive zeros there is a block of one or more positive values. Replace each block (together with its closing zero) by a single node holding the sum of the block, and remove all zeros. Return the values of the new list.

For [0,3,1,0,4,5,2,0] the blocks are [3,1] and [4,5,2], so the answer is [4,11]. Try to do it by reusing the existing nodes with one pass.
constraints: nums[0] = 0 and nums[nums.length - 1] = 0, and no two zeros are adjacent
1 ≤ nums[i] ≤ 1,000 for every non-zero value (so every sum fits in 32 bits)
hints: Every zero ends one block and begins the next one. There is one result node per block.
Walk through the list keeping a running sum. Add each positive value to it. What should happen when you meet a zero?

Skip the leading zero. At every later zero, the running sum is complete: write it into a result node (or overwrite the first node of the block in place) and reset the sum to 0. The last zero finishes the last block.
editorial: Scan once with a running sum s. A positive value is added to s. A zero closes the current block: append s to the result and reset s to 0. The very first zero closes an empty block, so skip it (or start the scan at the second node). With real nodes you can reuse them: keep a tail pointer into the output, store s into the first node of the block and link tail.next to the closing zero's successor; here we only need the final values.

The pass is O(n) time. Extra space is O(1) when relinking nodes in place, and O(k) for k blocks when you build a separate result. Because the values are at most 1,000 and the list holds at most 5,000 nodes, a block sum is at most 5 * 10<sup>6</sup>.
